rows.evidence: Registry: 10.1111/j.1540-6261.1997.tb03807.x, 'The Limits of Arbitrage', Shleifer; Vishny, The Journal of Finance 52(1) 35-55, 1997. Crossref and Wiley were not reachable (proxy 403; WebFetch permission refused for onlinelibrary.wiley.com and api.crossref.org). Checked against the JSTOR-stamped article PDF at https://ms.mcmaster.ca/%7Egrasselli/ShleiferVishny97.pdf: header 'The Journal of Finance, Vol. 52, No. 1. (Mar., 1997), pp. 35-55', title and authors match. Abstract (verbatim): 'Textbook arbitrage in financial markets requires no capital and entails no risk. In reality, almost all arbitrage requires capital, and is typically risky. Moreover, professional arbitrage is conducted by a relatively small number of highly specialized investors using other people's capital. Such professional arbitrage has a number of interesting implications for security pricing, including the possibility that arbitrage becomes ineffective in extreme circumstances, when prices diverge far from fundamental values.' The spans in L01 line 303 and L02 line 235 restate this ('who invest other people's money ... can become ineffective in extreme circumstances, when prices diverge far from fundamental values'); attribution correct at locator 'Abstract'. The builder's limitation (worded to the abstract) is confirmed: the wording stays inside the abstract. Grade and key-results wording are separate rows.

Registry: 10.1111/jofi.12620, 'Deviations from Covered Interest Rate Parity', Du; Tepper; Verdelhan, The Journal of Finance 73(3) 915-957, 2018. Checked on RePEc https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v73y2018i3p915-957.html (JF 73(3) 915-957, June 2018, DOI 10.1111/jofi.12620) and MIT DSpace https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/128481. Abstract: 'We find that deviations from the covered interest rate parity (CIP) condition imply large, persistent, and systematic arbitrage opportunities in one of the largest asset markets in the world. Contrary to the common view, these deviations for major currencies are not explained away by credit risk or transaction costs. They are particularly strong for forward contracts that appear on banks' balance sheets at the end of the quarter, pointing to a causal effect of banking regulation on asset prices.' The L01 span restates each clause (large, persistent, systematic; not explained by credit risk or transaction costs for major currencies; strong for contracts on balance sheets at quarter-end; causal effect of banking regulation). Attribution correct at 'Abstract'. Sample: the May 2017 working-paper version (https://www.bportugal.pt/sites/default/files/cme2017_7.pdf) uses G10 currencies, Libor basis January 2000 to September 2016, 'very close to zero for all G10 currencies before 2007'; the span does not state the sample or period (row grade-du2018deviations).

The problem asks to 'State and prove the version of Proposition 2.2' for bid-ask costs. The solution states 'There is no theta with X theta = 0 and c(theta) < 0 iff c(theta) >= 0 for every theta in ker X' and itself calls this 'a tautology as stated'. So no version of Proposition 2.2 is stated or proved; the rest is a correct discussion of the structure of c (I re-derived p^a t^+ - p^b t^- = p^b t + (p^a - p^b) t^+, convexity, positive homogeneity, and c(theta) + c(-theta) = sum (p^a_n - p^b_n)|theta_n|). The analogue of Proposition 2.2 is a kernel condition on prices: there is no zero-payoff portfolio with negative cost iff some price vector p~ with p^b <= p~ <= p^a satisfies p~ ⊥ ker X. §6 bullet 1 promises this ('the law of one price becomes a pair of inequalities. Problem R1 works this out'), and the solution does not deliver it. The subadditivity justification is also garbled: '(a+b)^+ <= a^+ + b^+ and (a+b)^- <= a^- + b^-' does not give subadditivity of p^a t^+ - p^b t^- on its own (the second term enters with a minus sign); convexity of the rewritten form does.
rows.fix: Replace the statement with: 'c(theta) >= 0 for every theta in ker X iff there is p~ in R^N with p^b <= p~ <= p^a and p~^T theta = 0 for all theta in ker X.' Prove (<=) directly (p^a t^+ - p^b t^- >= p~ t for p^b <= p~ <= p^a, so c(theta) >= p~^T theta = 0) and (=>) by LP duality or Farkas (a forward reference to Lesson 3's duality is acceptable if stated as such). Derive subadditivity from convexity plus positive homogeneity rather than from the two inequalities.
